text: Commonly inflamed organs and causes: joints (arthritis) — from injury, or microbes like Streptococcus entering via wounds (e.g. teeth clipping, tail docking in piglets) and later reaching the joint; intestine (enteritis) — from bacteria like E. coli or Salmonella damaging the gut wall, or irritants like sand eaten by young animals; bladder (cystitis) — from infection, or from mineral 'stones' forming when animals don't drink enough, irritating the bladder (in sows this shows as small, painful jets of urine, sometimes ending with a little pus); trachea/bronchi (tracheitis/bronchitis) — from microbes like Mycoplasma damaging the lining, or irritant gases like ammonia from un-removed manure, both causing strong coughing; and eyes (conjunctivitis) — painful, closed eyelids, red/swollen conjunctiva, and discharge. Usage guidance: for inflammation from systemic infection (diarrhea, pneumonia, septicemia), inject an antibiotic combined with Dexamethasone; for local inflammation (joint, udder), inject Dexamethasone separately at a higher dose (typically 1–2 mg per 50 kg). Do not use anti-inflammatory drugs on an abscess — once it turns fluid/soft, it should simply be opened for drainage — or on a fresh wound, since inflammation is part of normal healing there. Non-steroidal drugs are often used specifically for fever and pain rather than inflammation itself — for example, treating a painful leg in a lame sow lets her stand, eat, and drink again, and reducing high fever generally helps recovery by letting the animal feel well enough to eat and drink. Dexamethasone also treats allergic reactions — e.g. skin redness/itching from insect bites in pigs, or photosensitivity skin lesions in cattle after eating certain plants (inject early once lesions start), and severe allergic/anaphylactic-type reactions after vaccination (e.g. some sows react to Aujeszky vaccine with nervousness, red skin, rapid breathing, heavy salivation, and in serious cases collapse and unconsciousness — Dexamethasone should be injected urgently).
